draft.title: Writing about a text
card: A claim is the point you argue about the text. It answers the question and says something specific, not just what happens.
Evidence is a short detail from the text that supports the claim. A few well-chosen words, or a brief description of a moment, work better than a long passage.
Explanation shows how the evidence proves the claim. It says what the detail suggests and why that matters to the claim.
A strong paragraph uses all three. Evidence with no explanation leaves the reader to guess your point, and a claim with no evidence is only an opinion.
draft.remember: Claim what you think, show it with short evidence, then explain how the evidence proves it.

a.q: What is the job of explanation in a paragraph about a text?
opts: It shows how the evidence supports the claim
It retells the events around the evidence
It repeats the claim in the same words
It adds a second quote to fill the space
a.why: Explanation links the evidence back to the claim by saying what the detail suggests. Retelling events is tempting, but it only repeats what happens and does not show how the evidence proves anything.
a.clue: Think about what connects evidence to the claim.

b.q: Priya writes: 'Mara is lonely.' She then describes how Mara eats dinner alone each night in the novel. She stops there. What is the main weakness in her paragraph?
opts: She has not explained how the detail shows loneliness
She has used evidence that is too short
She has not made a claim about the character
She has used a detail instead of a long passage
b.why: Priya has a claim and a detail, but she never says how eating alone shows loneliness. Short evidence is not a fault, because the card says brief details work better than long ones.
b.clue: Check which of the three parts is missing.

a.best: It shows how the evidence supports the claim

b.best: She has not explained how the detail shows loneliness
